claims.text: The deployment: 'The United States Air Force conducted a test of a special light-sensitive telescope high up in the coastal mountains in the Los Padres National Forest above Big Sur, California, between August and November 1964. The objective was to collect low-light-level photography of missile launches into the Air Force Western Test Range from Vandenberg Air Force Base, situated a little over 100 miles to the south... Nine of eleven launches from Vandenberg were successfully covered during the three-month deployment.'

desc: THE RAREST EVIDENTIARY SHAPE IN THIS CLUSTER: TWO PARTICIPANTS, BOTH PUBLISHED UNDER THEIR OWN NAMES, AGREEING ABOUT THE FACTS OF THE DEPLOYMENT AND DISAGREEING ABOUT ITS PRODUCT. The Air Force placed a borrowed 24-inch Boston University telescope, mounted on a modified five-inch gun mount and fitted with an image orthicon television camera tube, at about 4,000 feet in the Los Padres National Forest above Big Sur, and covered nine of eleven Vandenberg launches between August and November 1964. Lt. Robert Jacobs, named on-site commander by the 1369th Photographic Squadron, published in January 1989 that the resulting film showed a saucer-shaped object circling an Atlas warhead and firing a beam at it. Kingston A. George, the project engineer, published in Winter 1993 that the event was at dawn on 22 September 1964 on a launch nicknamed 'Buzzing Bee', that what was recorded was decoy and chaff deployment giving away the false status of the decoys, that the classified alarm which followed concerned the vulnerability of a weapons system rather than anything extraterrestrial, that Jacobs was not authorised to view the imagery, and that the film was destroyed long before its twelve-year declassification date. George cites a contemporaneous internal document by title and date, which is the best unopened lead this pass produced.

timeline.label: Atlas launch 'Buzzing Bee' filmed from Big Sur at dawn
timeline.text: The project engineer's published account fixes the event at dawn on 22 September 1964, on an Atlas launch nicknamed 'Buzzing Bee', photographed by a borrowed Boston University 24-inch telescope with an image orthicon tube sited in the Los Padres National Forest above Big Sur. Lt. Robert Jacobs, the on-site commander, later published that the film showed a saucer-shaped object firing a beam at the warhead; the project engineer published that it showed decoy deployment and trailing packing material. Jacobs's own article gives the date as 2, 3 or 15 September 1964.

timeline.label: Contemporaneous Air Force staff study on the Big Sur imagery
timeline.text: 'Preliminary Report on Image Orthicon Photography from Big Sur', Headquarters 1st Strategic Aerospace Division Operations Analysis Staff Study, 13 October 1964, by Kingston A. George. Cited by title and date in his 1993 article. NOT OPENED. It is the best unopened lead this cluster produced: a contemporaneous Air Force document about the filming, written three weeks afterwards.

timeline.label: The project engineer answers Jacobs in print
timeline.text: Kingston A. George, 'The Big Sur UFO: An Identified Flying Object', Skeptical Inquirer, Vol. 17, No. 2, Winter 1993, pages 180 to 186. He identifies himself as the project engineer, confirms that Jacobs was named on-site commander by the 1369th Photo Squadron, publishes team photographs, fixes the date and launch, explains the imagery as decoy and chaff deployment, and states that Jacobs was not authorised to view the film.
